messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sameer had been a tax consultant for a decade before he took the sabbatical. He wanted, for once, to do something that felt unequivocally good. The six months with the international relief agency were meant to be that. The end of his tour was just three weeks away when the marketplace was hit. He remembers the sequence in fragments, a deck of cards thrown in the air. There was the loud, calm voice of a local official arguing with a vendor, a flash of anger in his eyes. Then the concussion of the blast, a force that threw him against a wall. He remembers the ground, the grit in his mouth, and curling into a ball with his arms over his head. The smell is what stays with him most—a choking mix of burning plastic, dust, and something else, something acrid and sweet. When he could finally look up, the world was grey smoke and screams. He saw things he doesn't allow himself to fully recall, but the feeling of it is always there: a profound, gut-wrenching certainty that he should have done more, that he was there to help and had instead just hidden on the ground while others died. He believes he failed them.

Returning home to his wife and his quiet suburban life was a jarring dislocation. The world he had known, one governed by rules, logic, and a basic sense of fairness, felt like a distant memory, a story someone else had told him. This new world was menacing and unpredictable. Back in his office, the ordinary sounds of life became threats. A car door slamming in the parking lot would cause him to flinch so violently he’d knock over his coffee. His concentration, once his greatest professional asset, was shattered. He would stare at a client’s financial records, the numbers blurring into meaningless shapes, his mind snagged on the image of a child’s shoe lying in the rubble. He began making mistakes, missing deductions, and had to ask his manager to double-check all his filings, a humiliating admission of his new incompetence.

The triggers were everywhere. One afternoon, a client grew frustrated, his voice rising in calm but firm anger over a tax liability. Sameer felt the air leave his lungs. He saw not a disgruntled accountant but the furious official in the market, seconds before the explosion. He had to excuse himself, locking himself in a bathroom stall, his hands pressed over his face until the shaking subsided. He started avoiding client meetings, conducting all business over email. The smell of a neighbor’s bonfire one evening sent him into a full-blown panic, forcing him to retreat to the basement. When a colleague’s father passed away, he couldn’t bring himself to attend the funeral; the very thought of being in a place so explicitly dedicated to grief was unbearable.

His life began to shrink. He had come to believe that he didn’t deserve happiness, not after what he’d witnessed, not after his failure. He and his wife had planned a trip to celebrate their anniversary, but he cancelled it, telling her he was too busy with work. The truth was, the idea of relaxing on a beach, of feeling hopeful or joyful, felt like a betrayal of those who had lost everything. He felt utterly set apart from everyone, including his wife, as if he were living behind a thick wall of glass. At night, the feeling of threat was most acute. He would lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, certain that the darkness held some imminent danger. Often, a memory would surface—not as a story, but as a bodily sensation. He would find himself unconsciously tensing, his arms creeping up to shield his head, his body reenacting the posture of terror he held on the dusty ground. Each time, a wave of shame would wash over him, hot and suffocating.

It was his wife who finally broke through the isolation. She found him one night, sitting alone in the dark living room long after she had gone to bed. She didn’t speak, but simply sat with him, her presence a quiet question. In that moment, he realized how far he had drifted, not just from his old self, but from the person he loved most. He is seeking help now not because he believes he can be fixed—he is certain some things are permanently broken—but because he is terrified of losing what little he has left. He feels like a ghost in his own life and is holding on to the faint hope that therapy might help him learn how to live in it again.
